04

Optimization

Finding Better Solutions

Turn a real problem into one a computer can score, then search for better and better answers.

Many real-world problems have several possible solutions, but some are better than others. In this module, we use a delivery route problem to explore how computers represent, evaluate, and improve solutions. We begin with one route and learn how small changes can make it better. Then we explore how a genetic algorithm works with a population of solutions. Finally, we see how optimization is also used to improve AI systems.

Learning objectives

  • Model a real-world problem as an optimization problem: candidate solution, solution representation, objective function, search space and constraints.
  • Compute the objective value of a candidate solution, such as the length of a delivery route; say whether to minimize or maximize, whether the problem is discrete or continuous, and which wishes are constraints or soft preferences.
  • Trace single-solution local search (hill climbing) on a small route problem, and explain current solution, neighbouring solution, best solution found so far, local optimum and global optimum.
  • Trace one generation of a genetic algorithm on the same problem, keep every route valid, and compare population-based search with single-solution search.
  • Explain how optimization helps to build AI systems: gradient descent and the learning rate inside the model; hyperparameter tuning, feature selection and neural architecture search around it.

Key terms in this module

Optimization
Finding the best possible solution according to a defined objective, while satisfying any constraints that apply.
Travelling Salesperson Problem (TSP)
Find the shortest route that starts at a depot, visits every customer exactly once and returns to the depot. Module 3 and Lab 2 call it the travelling salesman problem; it is the same problem.
Problem modelling
Turning a real situation into a precise problem that a computer can work on: keep what matters (places, distances), drop the rest (traffic, the colour of the van).
Candidate solution
One complete answer, good or bad, such as one full route. In Module 3 a solution was a path built step by step; here it is one complete answer, judged as a whole.
Solution representation
How a candidate solution is written so that an algorithm can store it and change it: a permutation such as [A, C, B, D] for a route, or a bit string such as 1010 for yes/no choices.
Permutation
A list that contains every item exactly once, in some order, such as [A, C, B, D]. A permutation representation writes each route this way, so every customer is visited exactly once.
Decision variable
Something whose value we choose, such as which customer comes first in a route. A candidate solution gives a value to every decision variable.
Search space (solution space)
All the candidate solutions the representation allows. Four customers give 24 orders, which are 12 different routes, because a route and its reverse have the same length.
Objective function
A function that gives each candidate solution a number that measures its quality, such as the total distance of a route, including the return to the depot. It evaluates candidates; it does not choose which ones to try. It plays the role of Module 2's utility function, but it is not the PEAS performance measure. In machine learning it is called a loss function.
Search strategy
The part of a method that decides which candidate solutions to explore next, such as: swap two customers and try the new route.
Minimization / maximization
The direction of the search: minimize a cost, an error or a distance; maximize a profit, a benefit or a fitness. Maximizing f is the same as minimizing −f.
Constraint
A requirement that a solution must satisfy to be accepted at all, such as: no student has two exams at the same time. Section 2.3 calls it a hard requirement; Module 6 calls it a hard constraint.
Soft preference
A desirable condition that is not required, such as few students with two exams on one day. It enters the objective function as a penalty or a reward.
Penalty
An amount added to the objective each time a soft preference is not met, when the objective is minimized.
Feasible solution
A candidate solution that satisfies every constraint. All feasible solutions together form the feasible region, which is part of the search space.
Optimal solution
An optimal solution is a feasible solution for which no better feasible solution exists, according to the objective function.
Discrete optimization
Optimization where the decision variables take separate values: whole numbers, yes/no choices or orderings. Example: the order of visiting customers.
Continuous optimization
Optimization where the decision variables take real values anywhere in a range. Example: choosing x to minimize (x − 3)², or the weights of a model.
Local search
A family of methods that move between candidate solutions, using a neighbourhood or other small changes, to improve the objective. They usually do not keep the path that led to the answer.
Single-solution search
Methods that hold and improve one candidate solution at a time, such as hill climbing.
Population-based search
Methods that hold and improve a group of candidate solutions at a time, such as genetic algorithms. The members are candidate solutions, not agents.
Neighbourhood
The candidate solutions reachable from the current one by one small, defined change, such as swapping two customers in a route. Each of them is a neighbouring solution (a neighbour). Not the same as the nearest neighbour method of Lab 2, where a neighbour is a place.
Neighbouring solution
A candidate solution one small change away from the current one, such as a route with two customers swapped.
Current solution
The candidate solution a single-solution method holds now and tries to improve.
Best solution found so far
The best solution found during the search. Some methods need to store it separately because their current solution may become worse.
Hill climbing
Single-solution local search: move to the best neighbour, and stop when no neighbour is better. Better means shorter for a route, higher for a fitness.
Stopping criterion
The rule that ends a search loop: no neighbour is better (hill climbing), the step is tiny or a step limit is reached (gradient descent), or a fixed number of generations (genetic algorithm).
Local optimum
A solution that no neighbour improves. It may also be the global optimum, or a better solution may exist elsewhere. It is a local maximum or a local minimum, depending on the direction.
Global optimum
The best feasible solution of the whole problem: the global maximum when maximizing, the global minimum when minimizing.
Landscape
A picture of a problem: each position is a candidate solution, and the height is its objective value.
Plateau say: pla-TOH
A flat area where all neighbours have the same value, so the search has no direction to follow.
Ridge
A narrow line along which the objective improves, but every single move the neighbourhood allows makes it worse, so the search stops early.
Random-restart hill climbing
Running hill climbing many times from new random starting solutions and keeping the best solution found so far.
Simulated annealing say: a-NEE-ling
Optional reading. A variant of hill climbing that sometimes accepts a worse neighbour on purpose, often at first and rarely later, to escape a local optimum.
Nature-inspired optimization
Optimization methods that take their main idea from a process in nature: biological evolution (genetic algorithms), swarms (particle swarm and ant colony optimization) or physical annealing (simulated annealing). Some keep a population and some keep one solution at a time; a natural origin does not make a method better.
Genetic algorithm
Population-based search that repeats: population → evaluation → selection → crossover → mutation → new population.
Population
The group of candidate solutions a genetic algorithm holds at one time. Each round of the cycle produces a new generation.
Chromosome (individual)
How one candidate solution is written in a genetic algorithm: a route list such as [A, C, B, D], or a bit string such as 1010. One member of the population is called an individual.
Fitness function
The score a genetic algorithm gives each chromosome, where higher is better. If the objective is a distance or a cost, the fitness must turn it around: a shorter route is fitter, for example fitness = 1 / distance.
Selection
Choosing parents at random, with fitter chromosomes more likely to be chosen. One simple way: pick two at random and keep the fitter one.
Crossover
Making a child from parts of two parents. For routes it must keep a permutation: no customer twice, none missing. It does not guarantee a better child.
Mutation
A small random change to a chromosome: swap two customers in a route, or flip one bit. It keeps variety in the population, and can make a child better or worse.
Derivative (gradient)
The slope of the objective at the current point: which way is uphill and how steep. With one variable it is f′(x); with many it is the gradient, one slope for each variable.
Gradient descent
Continuous optimization that repeats x ← x − α·f′(x): a step against the slope. It is how models are trained. With a suitable learning rate the objective goes down; with one that is too large it can go up.
Learning rate
α, the size of each step in gradient descent. Too small is slow; too large jumps over the minimum and may never settle. It is a hyperparameter, chosen by experiment.
Hyperparameter tuning
Searching for the best settings that are chosen before training, such as the learning rate or the number of layers. Each candidate is scored by training a model and testing it on validation data.
Feature selection
Choosing which inputs (features) a model should use. A candidate is a bit string with one bit per feature; the objective is the score on validation data.
Neural architecture search
Searching for a good design of a neural network: how many layers, of what kind, and how they connect. Research has used evolutionary algorithms and other methods for it.
Section 4.1

Optimization: From Problems to Solutions

Many real-world problems have more than one possible solution. The challenge is to find a better one.

Imagine you are a delivery driver. You start at the depot, visit four customers, A, B, C and D, and return to the depot. You must visit every customer exactly once. In which order should you visit them? Different people suggest different orders. (In the lecture, each of you suggested one.)

Here are the distances between the places. They are illustrative: small whole numbers, in kilometres, chosen so that you can add them by hand. They are not real map distances, and the distance from X to Y is the same as from Y to X.

kmDepotABCD
Depot—6428
A6—473
B44—45
C274—6
D8356—

Take two suggestions. The first visits A, then C, then B, then D:

Follow the arrows from the depot and back. The map only shows the order; it is not drawn to scale.

[A, C, B, D] 6 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 30 km

[A, D, B, C] 6 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 20 km

Both routes follow the rules of the job: every customer is visited exactly once, and the driver returns to the depot. But the second route is 10 km shorter, so it is better. That raises the real question of this module: can we find an even shorter route?

Optimization is the process of finding the best possible solution according to a defined objective, while satisfying any constraints that apply.

Our two routes show three levels of success:

  1. An acceptable solution

    It follows all the rules: every customer once, and back to the depot. Both routes are acceptable.

  2. A better solution

    It is acceptable, and it is shorter. [A, D, B, C] is better than [A, C, B, D].

  3. An optimal solution

    An optimal solution is a feasible solution for which no better feasible solution exists. (Feasible means that it follows all the rules.) We do not know yet whether [A, D, B, C] is optimal.

The methods in this module move from level 1 towards level 3. They aim for a good solution. Finding a good solution does not prove that it is optimal: there may be a better one that the method has not tried.

We have compared two routes by hand. But how can a computer represent and evaluate thousands of possible routes? We need to describe the problem precisely, one step at a time.

Problem modelling

The first step is problem modelling: turning a real situation into a precise problem that a computer can work on. We keep what matters: the places and the distances between them. We drop the rest: traffic, the size of the van. Module 3 called this dropping of details abstraction.

Our model is the Travelling Salesperson Problem (TSP). Module 3 and Lab 2 call it the travelling salesman problem; it is the same problem. It is a simplified version of real delivery.

Candidate solutions

Each route suggested for the driver is a candidate solution: one complete answer, good or bad. [A, C, B, D] is a candidate, and so is [A, D, B, C]. We judge each one as a whole.

i
You have already met optimization

In Module 3, uniform-cost search and A* (with an admissible heuristic) return a cheapest path. That is optimization over paths. The two modules ask their questions in different ways:

  • Module 3: How can we find a path, or a sequence of actions, that reaches a goal?
  • Module 4: How can we represent, evaluate and improve candidate solutions?

This is a difference of focus for teaching, not a strict line between search and optimization. The delivery problem fits both: Lab 2 builds a route one customer at a time, like a path; this module takes complete routes and improves them.

Solution representation

A computer needs a fixed way to write a candidate down, so that it can store it and change it. This is the solution representation. A route is written as a list of the customers in visiting order, such as [A, C, B, D]. The depot is not written, because every route starts and ends there.

A list that contains every item exactly once, in some order, is a permutation. The things we choose are called the decision variables: here, which customer comes first, second, third and fourth. For yes/no choices, such as which projects to fund, a bit string such as 1010 is common.

Objective function

To compare routes, the computer needs a number for each one. An objective function gives each candidate solution a number that measures its quality. Here it is the total distance of the route, including the last leg back to the depot:

Route Depot → A → C → B → D → Depot

Objective 6 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 30 km

A shorter route is better, so we minimize the distance. Other problems maximize instead: a profit, a benefit or a fitness. Maximizing f is the same as minimizing −f. The genetic algorithm in section 4.3 talks about fitness, where higher is better; it simply turns "shorter" into "fitter".

The same shape of question, seen from two sides. Which side you are on depends on how you defined the objective.
i
The objective function is not the PEAS performance measure

The performance measure of section 2.3 judges an agent's behaviour from the outside, over its whole working life: did the deliveries arrive, safely and on time? The objective function scores one candidate solution inside an optimization method: how long is this route? The designer often builds the objective from the performance measure, but the two do different jobs.

Constraints

At the start we said that both routes follow the rules of the job. Those rules are the constraints. A constraint is a requirement that a solution must satisfy to be accepted at all. For the driver: every customer is visited exactly once, and the route starts and ends at the depot. A candidate that satisfies every constraint is a feasible solution.

Not every wish is a constraint. A soft preference is a desirable condition that is not required. Suppose customer C is a pharmacy, and we would like to visit it early. A route that visits C last can still be used; it is just worse. So the wish enters the objective function: for every customer visited before C, we add a penalty. (When we maximize, meeting a preference can add a reward instead.)

The same line appears in an exam timetable. "No student has two exams at the same time" is a constraint. "Few students with two exams on one day" is a soft preference. Section 2.3 drew this line with different words: hard requirements and things to improve. Module 6 calls the first kind hard constraints.

!
A constraint is not just a large penalty

"No student has two exams at the same time" must always hold. If you write it only as a small penalty, the search may accept a clash to save a few points somewhere else. Keep what must hold as a constraint, and put only the preferences into the objective.

Search space

How many routes could the driver choose from? The search space is all the candidate solutions the representation allows. Four customers can be put in order in 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways. A route and the same route driven backwards have the same length, so there are only 12 different routes.

Twelve routes can be checked by hand. With 10 customers there are 3,628,800 orders, and the number grows very fast; Lab 2 measures how fast. That is why we need methods that look for a good route without trying them all.

Are all the candidates in the search space acceptable? Not always. The feasible solutions together form the feasible region, and it is only part of the search space.

The feasible region sits inside the search space. The objective function scores one candidate at a time.
Do not mix up

Search space and feasible region

  • The search space holds every candidate the representation allows
  • The feasible region keeps only the candidates that satisfy all constraints
  • The final answer must be in the feasible region
Do not mix up

Constraint and objective

  • A constraint is yes or no: a solution either satisfies it or is not accepted
  • The objective is a number: lower (or higher) is better
  • A constraint is never traded for a better objective value

For the driver, the two are the same. A permutation visits each customer exactly once, so every route we can write is feasible: the representation makes the constraint impossible to break. A weaker representation, such as "any list of four letters", would also allow [A, A, B, D], and the method would have to reject or penalize it.

One more question about the search space: are its candidates separate, or is there something in between?

Discrete optimization: the decision variables take separate values, such as whole numbers, yes/no choices, or orderings.

Continuous optimization: the decision variables take real values anywhere in a range.

Swipe sideways to see all columns →

ProblemRepresentationType
Order of visiting 4 customersa permutation, such as [A, C, B, D]Discrete
Which of 4 projects to fund within a budgeta bit string, such as 1010Discrete
Minimize f(x) = (x − 3)²a real number xContinuous
Discrete: separate candidates with nothing in between. Continuous: a smooth range of candidates.

The type depends on the decision variables, not on the method. Section 2.4 used the same words for the states and actions of an environment. Discrete does not mean finite: a variable that can be any whole number is discrete, yet it has infinitely many values.

Search strategy

We can now write a route, score it, and check the rules. One question is left: which route should the computer try next? That is the job of the search strategy: it decides which candidate solutions to explore. For example: swap two customers and try the new route.

Do not mix up

Objective function

  • Evaluates one candidate solution
  • Gives it a number: [A, C, B, D] → 30 km
  • Is part of the problem
Do not mix up

Search strategy

  • Decides which candidate solutions to explore
  • For example: swap two customers and try the new route
  • Is part of the method (sections 4.2 and 4.3)

Many search strategies belong to local search: a family of methods that move between candidate solutions, using a neighbourhood or other small changes, to improve the objective. They care about the quality of the final solution, so they usually do not keep the path that led to it. This module compares two kinds:

One candidate

Single-solution search

  • Holds one candidate solution at a time
  • Changes it a little and keeps the change if it is better
  • Example: hill climbing (section 4.2)
A group of candidates

Population-based search

  • Holds a group of candidate solutions at a time
  • Builds new candidates from the better ones
  • Example: genetic algorithms (section 4.3)
Single-solution methods improve one candidate. Population-based methods improve a group.

These are two useful families, not a complete list. The nearest neighbour method of Lab 2 does not improve complete routes at all: it builds one route, customer by customer. Strictly speaking, genetic algorithms belong to evolutionary optimization rather than to local search; this course places them here because they solve the same kind of problem.

Putting it together

The steps of this section, with the delivery problem under each one. Steps 5 and 6 repeat until the solution is good enough.

Sections 4.2 and 4.3 now show two ways to do step 5.

Where you meet these problems

🚚 Delivery routes

Parcels, food and medicine. Real companies add delivery times, many vans and live traffic.

📅 Timetables and rosters

Exams, lectures, shifts in a hospital. Only the final schedule is judged.

🚑 Where to place facilities

Ambulance stations, warehouses, or mobile towers in a city, placed to reduce distance for everyone.

🤖 Building AI systems

Training a model and choosing its settings are optimization problems too. Section 4.4 shows how.

Check yourself

Using the distance table, find the total distance of the route [D, B, A, C]. Is it better than [A, C, B, D]? Then: how many different orders are there for 5 customers?

Show answer

Depot → D 8, D → B 5, B → A 4, A → C 7, C → Depot 2: 26 km. It is better than [A, C, B, D] (30 km), because it is shorter. If you got 24, you forgot the last leg back to the depot.

Five customers can be ordered in 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 ways. A route and its reverse have the same length, so there are 60 different routes.

Check yourself

The Red Crescent in Jeddah has 10 possible sites for new ambulance stations. At least one station must be built, and the budget allows at most 3. They want the average time to reach a caller to be as small as possible. Name the representation, the search space, the constraint, the objective function and its direction, and the type of problem. Then: what changes if a station may be placed at any point on the map?

Show answer

Representation: a bit string of 10 bits, one per site: 1 = build a station there, 0 = do not. Search space: all bit strings of length 10, 210 = 1024 candidates. Constraint: at least 1 and at most 3 stations, so the feasible region holds only 175 of the 1024 candidates (10 with one station, 45 with two, 120 with three). Objective function: the average time to reach a caller; direction: minimize. Type: discrete optimization.

Now suppose you will build exactly 3 stations, and each may be placed anywhere on the map. Each station needs its own pair of coordinates (x, y), so you choose three pairs: six real numbers. The problem becomes continuous optimization.

18 min read

Section 4.2

Single-Solution Local Search

This section studies one idea: improve one candidate solution by small changes. We use hill climbing, the simplest example, on the delivery problem of section 4.1. Hill climbing will reach the 20 km route from section 4.1 by itself, and then we will see why it stops there.

Neighbouring routes

We already have a 30 km route. Can we improve it without starting from scratch? One simple idea is to change the order of just two customers and see whether the new route is shorter. For example, swapping C and D in [A, C, B, D] gives [A, D, B, C]. Each route you can reach with one swap is a neighbouring solution, or neighbour. All of them together are the neighbourhood of the route.

Four customers give 6 pairs to swap (A–B, A–C, A–D, B–C, B–D, C–D), so every route has exactly 6 neighbours. Swapping keeps a permutation, so every neighbour is still a valid route.

!
Two meanings of "neighbour"

In Lab 2, the nearest neighbour method drives to the closest customer not yet visited: a neighbour there is a place. In this section a neighbour is a route: the route you get after one swap. When the meaning is not clear, say "neighbouring route".

Hill climbing

One loop, repeated. The search holds one route at a time.
  1. Current solution

    The route the search holds now. It starts as a random or simple route.

  2. Generate neighbours

    Make every route that is one swap away.

  3. Evaluate

    Compute the total distance of each neighbour.

  4. Compare

    Is the shortest neighbour shorter than the current route?

  5. Update

    If yes, it becomes the current solution: repeat from step 2. If no, stop. This rule is the stopping criterion.

Climbing sand dunes in thick fog

You want the highest point in the dunes, but you can only feel the ground one metre around you. So you always step upward. Eventually every direction goes down, and you stop.

You are standing on a top. Whether it is the top, you have no way of knowing: the fog never lifts.

The name comes from this maximization picture, where better means higher. For routes, better means shorter, so we climb "down" towards smaller distances. The idea is the same.

Tracing it on the delivery problem

Step 1. The current solution is [A, C, B, D], 30 km. Its six neighbours:

SwapNeighbouring routeTotal distance
A and C[C, A, B, D]26
A and B[B, C, A, D]26
A and D[D, C, B, A]28
C and B[A, B, C, D]28
C and D[A, D, B, C]20
B and D[A, C, D, B]28

Check one of them yourself: [A, D, B, C] is 6 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 20 km. The shortest neighbour, 20 km, is shorter than 30 km, so the search moves: [A, D, B, C] becomes the current solution.

Step 2. The current solution is [A, D, B, C], 20 km. Its six neighbours:

SwapNeighbouring routeTotal distance
A and D[D, A, B, C]21
A and B[B, D, A, C]21
A and C[C, D, B, A]23
D and B[A, B, D, C]23
D and C[A, C, B, D]30
B and C[A, D, C, B]23

No neighbour is shorter than 20 km, so hill climbing stops and returns [A, D, B, C], 20 km.

Is that the shortest route? There are only 12 different routes, so we can check them all. The shortest is [B, A, D, C]: 4 + 4 + 3 + 6 + 2 = 19 km. Why did hill climbing stop at 20 km when a 19 km route exists? Because no single swap of [A, D, B, C] gives a shorter route: in the step 2 table, every neighbour is 21 km or more. Hill climbing stopped because of the neighbourhood it was given, not because it found the best answer.

The loop as code

def hill_climbing(problem):
    current = problem.initial_solution()
    while True:
        neighbours = problem.neighbours(current)
        if not neighbours:
            return current          # no neighbours at all: stop
        best = min(neighbours, key=problem.cost)
        if problem.cost(best) >= problem.cost(current):
            return current          # no neighbour is better: stop
        current = best

The code does not know anything about routes. To use it for a problem, you write two functions: neighbours (for routes: all swaps) and cost (for routes: the total distance). To maximize instead, use max and <=.

Five words to keep apart

  1. Current solution

    The route the search holds now. In step 2 above: [A, D, B, C].

  2. Neighbouring solution

    A route one swap away from the current solution, such as [D, A, B, C].

  3. Best solution found so far

    The best solution found during the search. Some methods need to store it separately because their current solution may become worse.

  4. Local optimum

    A solution that no neighbour improves: [A, D, B, C], 20 km. It may also be the best of all, or a better solution may exist elsewhere.

  5. Global optimum

    The best solution of the whole problem: [B, A, D, C], 19 km. It is always a local optimum too. When maximizing, the two are called a local maximum and a global maximum; when minimizing, a local minimum and a global minimum.

In plain hill climbing the two are always the same, because the search only moves to better routes. They can differ in the methods below: random restarts start again from a new route, and simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse one.

Where hill climbing gets stuck

Drawn for maximization. For a distance, turn the picture upside down: the good places are the valleys.

A picture like this is called a landscape: each position is a candidate solution, and the height is its objective value. Hill climbing only knows the ground under its feet, never the whole map. Besides a local optimum, two other shapes can stop it:

  • Plateau: a flat area where all neighbours have the same value, so there is no direction to follow.
  • Ridge: the objective improves along a narrow line, but every single move the neighbourhood allows makes it slightly worse.

Random restarts

Different starting routes lead to different local optima. So run hill climbing again from a new random route, and keep the best result. This is random-restart hill climbing.

Swipe sideways to see all columns →

RunStartMovesStops atBest found so far
1[A, C, B, D], 30swap C and D → 20[A, D, B, C], 20[A, D, B, C], 20
2[A, B, C, D], 28swap A and C → 21,
swap B and D → 19		[C, D, A, B], 19[C, D, A, B], 19

Run 2 ends at [C, D, A, B]. That is [B, A, D, C] driven backwards: the same route, with the same length, 19 km. If a third run ended at 23 km, the best found so far would stay at 19. The program returns the best found so far, not the result of the last run.

i
Further exploration (optional): how many restarts?

Suppose one run finds the best solution with probability p, and the runs are independent. Then you need 1/p runs on average until the first success. That is an average, not a promise. With p = 0.1 you expect 10 runs, yet 10 runs succeed only about 65% of the time. This box is extra reading and is not tested.

Check yourself

Hill climbing holds [C, A, D, B], 21 km. Is it a local optimum? Check its six neighbours with the distance table of section 4.1.

Show answer

No. The six neighbours are 28 (swap C and A), 26 (C and D), 19 (C and B), 19 (A and D), 20 (A and B) and 26 (D and B). Two of them are shorter, so hill climbing moves on. The two 19 km neighbours, [B, A, D, C] and [C, D, A, B], are the same route driven in opposite directions.

Check yourself

Your route planner uses hill climbing from a random start. It returns a different route every time you run it, and the quality varies. Is this a bug?

Show answer

No. It starts from a random route, so it can stop at a different local optimum each time. The fix is not to remove the randomness but to use it: run the planner many times and keep the best route found so far. That is random-restart hill climbing.

i
Further exploration (optional): simulated annealing

Hill climbing never accepts a worse neighbour, and that is why it stops at a local optimum. Simulated annealing sometimes accepts a worse neighbour on purpose: often at the start, rarely near the end. In our example, from [A, D, B, C] (20 km) it might accept [B, D, A, C] (21 km). From there, swapping B and C gives [C, D, A, B], 19 km. One step back made a better route reachable. Because the method can leave a good route, it must keep the best solution found so far. The name comes from metalwork, where metal is heated and then cooled slowly so that it settles well. This box is extra reading and is not tested.

13 min read

Section 4.3

Population-Based Search: Genetic Algorithms

What if we keep several routes at once, instead of improving only one?

Remember where section 4.2 ended. From [A, C, B, D], hill climbing stopped at [A, D, B, C], 20 km, although [B, A, D, C] is only 19 km. One route can get stuck. Random restarts start again from a new route; a genetic algorithm takes another way.

Instead of improving one route, it keeps several routes and builds new ones from the better ones. A genetic algorithm explores several solutions at once, but it does not guarantee finding the best one.

A genetic algorithm repeats one cycle: Population → Evaluation → Selection → Crossover → Mutation → New population.

Selection keeps what works, crossover combines it, mutation keeps new options alive.
Breeding date palms

A farmer crosses a palm with excellent fruit and a palm that survives any heat, hoping for offspring with the good traits of both. Most offspring are ordinary. A few are better than either parent, and those become the parents of the next generation.

The cycle does the same with routes. Let us follow one generation on the delivery problem.

One generation on the delivery problem

Population and evaluation

We start with four routes. R1 is the starting route of section 4.2, and R3 is the route where hill climbing stopped.

RouteChromosomeTotal distance
R1[A, C, B, D]30
R2[C, A, D, B]21
R3[A, D, B, C]20
R4[A, B, C, D]28

These four routes form our first population: the group of candidate solutions the algorithm holds at one time. Each route is one individual, represented by a chromosome: for routes, the route list itself; for yes/no choices, a bit string such as 1010. An individual here is a candidate solution, not an intelligent agent: nothing in the population perceives or acts, so this is not the multi-agent setting of section 2.4.

Evaluation gives each chromosome a score with a fitness function, where higher is better. Our objective is a distance to minimize, so the fitness must turn it around: a shorter route has a higher fitness. One common choice is fitness = 1 / distance. In this example we only need to know which of two routes is fitter: the shorter one.

The best route found so far is R3, 20 km.

Selection

Selection chooses the parents. It is random, but fitter chromosomes are more likely to be chosen. One simple way: pick two routes at random and keep the fitter one, here the shorter one. In this run, the first draw compared R1 (30) with R2 (21) and chose R2. The second draw compared R4 (28) with R3 (20) and chose R3. A weak route can still be drawn, but it rarely wins.

Crossover

We have selected two parent routes. How can we use them to create a new route? The simplest idea is to cut both parents at the same place and join the parts. Cut R2 and R3 after position 2: [C, A] + [B, C] = [C, A, B, C]. Customer C appears twice and D is missing, so this is not a route at all.

Cutting works for bit strings, but it breaks a permutation. Crossover makes a child from parts of two parents, and for routes it must keep a permutation. One simple way:

  1. Keep the middle of parent 1

    Copy positions 2 and 3 of R2 into the child: [_, A, D, _].

  2. Fill the gaps in parent 2's order

    The missing customers are B and C. In R3 = [A, D, B, C], B comes before C. Fill the gaps from left to right: [B, A, D, C].

The child is a valid route: every customer appears exactly once. Its length is 4 + 4 + 3 + 6 + 2 = 19 km. With the roles of the parents swapped, the same rule keeps [_, D, B, _] from R3 and fills C, then A, in R2's order: a second child, [C, D, B, A], 23 km.

This rule is a simple version of order crossover (OX). The name does not matter for this course. What matters is that every child is still a valid route, with no customer repeated and none missing.

Mutation

Mutation is a small random change to a child. For routes it swaps two customers, the same move that made a neighbour in section 4.2. In this run it changed the second child: swapping D and A in [C, D, B, A] gives [C, A, B, D], 26 km. The child is still a valid route, but it is longer: mutation is random, and its job is to keep variety in the population, not to improve every child.

Cutting and swapping tails breaks a route. Keeping a part of one parent and filling the rest in the other parent's order always gives a valid route, and so does a swap.

New population

In this small example, the two children replace the two longest routes, R1 and R4. Other genetic algorithms replace the whole population.

Generation 1How it was madeTotal distance
[C, A, D, B]R2, kept21
[A, D, B, C]R3, kept20
[B, A, D, C]crossover of R2 and R319
[C, A, B, D]crossover of R3 and R2, then mutation26

The best route found so far improved from 20 km to 19 km, which is the global optimum of this small problem. The genetic algorithm combined the route where hill climbing stopped with another route, and found a shorter one. This was one lucky run: another run could do worse. With many customers, a genetic algorithm gives no guarantee of the global optimum.

!
Crossover and mutation do not guarantee a better child

The second child, [C, D, B, A] (23 km), is longer than both of its parents (21 and 20 km), and mutation then made it longer still. Good children survive because selection favours them, not because the operators are clever.

i
When a child breaks a constraint

With routes and a crossover that keeps a permutation, every child is feasible. With other representations it may not be: if each bit says whether to fund one project, a child can cost more than the budget. Three common rules:

  • Penalize it: keep it, but give it a very low fitness.
  • Reject it: throw it away and make a new child instead.
  • Repair it: change it until it satisfies the constraint, for example drop projects until the cost fits.

One solution or a population?

Hill climbing (4.2)Genetic algorithm (4.3)
Holdsone routea population of routes
Makes new routes byswapping two customerscrossover of two parents, then mutation
Uses the objective tocompare neighbours with the current routechoose parents and decide which routes stay
On our examplefrom [A, C, B, D] it stopped at 20 kmone generation reached 19 km
Main riskstops at the first local optimum it reachesmore work per step and more settings to choose, such as population size and mutation rate
Best found so farthe current route, unless you restartmust be stored: the population changes

Neither method is better in general. Hill climbing with random restarts also reached 19 km in section 4.2. The right choice depends on the problem, the representation and the computing time you have. The fair way to compare them is to run both on the same problem, with the same amount of work, several times, and compare the best routes they find.

i
Nature-Inspired Optimization: Learning from Nature

The farmer's idea is not only an analogy. Methods that take their main idea from a process in nature are called nature-inspired optimization. Three families:

  • Evolutionary algorithms copy biological evolution, like the genetic algorithm.
  • Swarm intelligence copies flocks of birds or ants leaving trails, like particle swarm optimization (PSO) and ant colony optimization (ACO).
  • Physics-inspired methods copy physical processes, like simulated annealing (the optional box in 4.2).

Nature-inspired does not mean population-based: simulated annealing improves one solution at a time. A natural origin does not make a method better or guarantee the global optimum.

Each family takes its idea from a different part of nature. The label under each one says how many candidates it holds.
Check yourself

Parents [A, C, D, B] (28 km) and [C, B, A, D] (21 km). (a) Cut both after position 2 and swap the tails: is the first child a valid route? (b) Use the crossover rule above, with [A, C, D, B] as parent 1. Write the child and its length. Is it better than both parents?

Show answer

(a) [A, C] + [A, D] = [A, C, A, D]. A appears twice and B is missing, so it is not a valid route.

(b) Keep [_, C, D, _]. The missing customers are A and B; in [C, B, A, D], B comes before A. The child is [B, C, D, A]: 4 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 6 = 23 km. It is shorter than the first parent (28) but longer than the second (21). Crossover mixes routes; it does not promise a better child.

13 min read

Section 4.4

Optimization in AI Development

Optimization is not only used to solve real-world problems. It can also help us build better AI systems. It does this in two places: inside a model, when the model is trained, and around a model, when we choose how to build it.

Training is continuous optimization inside the model. Design choices around the model are searched with the ideas of sections 4.1 to 4.3.

Inside the model: gradient descent

A machine learning model contains many numbers, called weights. Training means choosing the weights so that the model's answers are as good as possible on examples with known answers. The objective is called the loss: how wrong the answers are. We minimize it.

The weights are real numbers, so this is continuous optimization. A real number has infinitely many neighbours, so we cannot list them and compare them as in section 4.2. Instead we use the slope of the objective. Take a simple problem whose answer we already know, so we can watch the method find it:

Minimize f(x) = (x − 3)²

Slope: f′(x) = 2(x − 3)

The lowest value is at x = 3, where f(3) = 0.

  • The derivative f′(x) is the slope at the current point. It tells you which way is uphill and how steep it is. With many variables it becomes the gradient, one slope for each variable.
  • The learning rate α (alpha) is a small positive number that sets the size of each step.

Gradient descent repeats one update: $x_{\text{new}} = x - \alpha\, f'(x)$. The slope f′(x) points uphill, the minus sign turns the step downhill, and α is the learning rate. It stops when the step becomes tiny, or after a fixed number of steps.

Two steps by hand

Start at x = 0 with learning rate α = 0.1.

Swipe sideways to see all columns →

Stepxf(x)f′(x) = 2(x − 3)α · f′(x)new x
109−6−0.60 − (−0.6) = 0.6
20.65.76−4.8−0.480.6 − (−0.48) = 1.08

At x = 0 the slope is −6: the function goes down as x grows. The minus sign in the update turns that into a step to the right, towards 3. The steps get smaller on their own, because the slope gets flatter near the bottom.

The learning rate

The same function and the same start. Only the learning rate changes.

Too small (0.01), and the search is very slow. Reasonable (0.1), and it moves steadily towards 3. Too large (1.1), and it jumps over 3 and lands further away each time, so it never settles. There is no single correct learning rate; it is chosen by experiment. That choice is itself an optimization problem, as the next part shows.

Related to hill climbing, but not the same algorithm

Both improve one solution step by step, and both can stop at a local optimum: a function with several valleys can trap gradient descent in a local minimum. Hill climbing compares a list of neighbours and moves to the best one. Gradient descent never lists neighbours: it needs continuous variables and an objective whose slope we can compute, and it uses the slope to choose the direction. With a suitable learning rate, on a function with one valley such as (x − 3)², it approaches the global minimum.

Around the model: choosing how to build it

Building an AI model involves choices about its settings, inputs, and architecture. Optimization methods can help us explore these choices and find better configurations. Each choice follows the same steps as the delivery problem.

🎛️ Hyperparameter tuning

A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate α or the number of layers. A candidate solution is one combination of settings, for example α = 0.1 with 3 layers. Its objective value is how well the trained model does on validation data: examples kept aside, not used in training. Search methods try different combinations and keep the best.

🧮 Feature selection

Features are the inputs of a model, such as attendance or quiz marks when predicting a student's final result. Feature selection chooses which features to use. A candidate is a bit string, one bit per feature: 1 = use it. A neighbour flips one bit, so hill climbing works, and bit strings suit a genetic algorithm too.

🧠 Neural architecture search

The candidate is the design of a neural network: how many layers, of what kind, and how they connect. The objective is again performance on validation data, sometimes with size or speed. Research has explored such designs with evolutionary algorithms, and also with other methods.

Swipe sideways to see all columns →

ProblemCandidate solutionObjectiveDirection
Delivery routea permutation of the customerstotal distanceminimize
Hyperparameter tuninga combination of settingsscore on validation datamaximize
Feature selectiona bit string, one bit per featurescore on validation datamaximize
Neural architecture searcha network designscore on validation datamaximize

These are applications of optimization and search, not of one particular algorithm. One difference from the delivery problem matters a lot: to score one candidate here, you must train a model, which can take minutes or days. So these searches try far fewer candidates, and they choose them carefully.

Check yourself

(a) For f(x) = (x − 3)², start at x = 5 with α = 0.1 and compute one step. Then compute one step from the same start with α = 1.1. Which one helped? (b) A model can use 5 features. You want the set of features that gives the best score on validation data. Give the representation, the number of candidates, one neighbour of 10110, and the direction.

Show answer

(a) f′(5) = 2(5 − 3) = 4. With α = 0.1: x = 5 − 0.4 = 4.6, closer to 3. With α = 1.1: x = 5 − 4.4 = 0.6: it jumped over 3 and is now further away. The small rate helped; the large one made things worse.

(b) A bit string of 5 bits. There are 25 = 32 candidates (31 if at least one feature must be used). A neighbour flips one bit: for example 00110. The direction is maximize the validation score.

Revision card

Module 4 cheat sheet

From a real problem to a solution

  • Real-world problem → problem modelling → solution representation → objective function → search strategy → evaluation
  • Candidate solution — one complete answer, good or bad: one full route
  • Objective function evaluates a candidate · search strategy decides which candidates to explore
  • Objective function ≠ PEAS performance measure: one scores a candidate, the other judges the agent's behaviour
  • Constraint — must hold (yes or no) · soft preference — desirable, enters the objective as a penalty or a reward
  • Discrete or continuous: decided by the decision variables, not by the algorithm

The delivery example (TSP)

  • Representation: a permutation, such as [A, C, B, D]; the depot is not written
  • [A, C, B, D] = 6 + 7 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 30 km — count the last leg back to the depot
  • 4 customers: 24 orders, but 12 different routes (a route and its reverse have the same length)
  • Shortest route: [B, A, D, C], 19 km

Single-solution local search

  • Current solution → generate neighbours → evaluate → compare → update
  • Neighbour = swap two customers: 6 neighbours for 4 customers
  • [A, C, B, D] 30 → [A, D, B, C] 20 → stop: a local optimum, not the global optimum (19)
  • Random restarts: run hill climbing from different starting solutions and keep the best result.

Population-based search: genetic algorithm

  • Population → evaluation → selection → crossover → mutation → new population
  • Fitness: higher is better, so a shorter route is fitter
  • Cutting and swapping tails breaks a route: [C, A, B, C] has C twice and no D
  • Keep part of parent 1, fill the rest in parent 2's order: [B, A, D, C], a valid route
  • Mutation for routes: swap two customers — it can make a child worse

One solution or a population?

  • Hill climbing: one route, small changes, can stop at a local optimum
  • Genetic algorithm: many routes, combined and mutated, more work and more settings
  • Neither is better in general — compare them on the same problem with the same amount of work
  • Not every method is one of the two: the nearest neighbour method (Lab 2) builds a route instead of improving one

Optimization in AI development

  • Inside the model: gradient descent x ← x − α·f′(x) trains the weights
  • f(x) = (x − 3)², start 0, α = 0.1: x = 0 → 0.6 → 1.08
  • Learning rate too small: slow · too large (1.1): jumps over the minimum and never settles
  • Around the model: hyperparameter tuning · feature selection (a bit string) · neural architecture search

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Forgetting the last leg back to the depot
  • Saying hill climbing finds the best answer — it finds a local optimum
  • Returning the last solution instead of the best solution found so far
  • Giving a shorter route a lower fitness — fitness is higher for better routes
  • Cutting two routes and swapping the tails — a customer can appear twice or go missing
  • Mixing up the objective function (scores a candidate) and the search strategy (chooses what to try)
  • Saying gradient descent is hill climbing — it uses the slope instead of listing neighbours
